title: The mind's own country
hookLine: to his mother: wherever I go, the sky and my mind come with me (Consolation to Helvia 8)

cards: Same island. Same exile. Same man.
But a different letter. Before or after the one we read yesterday, nobody is sure which, Seneca wrote from Corsica to his mother, Helvia. It's a strange reversal.
Usually the person in trouble receives comfort. Here the exile is the one comforting. His mother had lost her husband, and now her son was gone too, to a rocky island across the sea.
So Seneca wrote to tell her he was all right, and why.

teach.b: First, a son consoles his mother. A consolation, Seneca knows, is usually written by someone safe at home to the one grieving. He says he's doing something new, writing as the one she's grieving for.

Second, people have always moved. Much of humanity lives far from where it was born, he reminds her: Greeks on the coasts of Italy, Romans in every province. Even Corsica has changed hands and peoples again and again.
Being away from home isn't a strange fate. It's an ordinary human thing.
Third, two things come along. The scholar Varro said that wherever we go, we have the same nature around us. Brutus said exiles may carry their own virtues with them.
Seneca puts them together: the world itself, and your own character, go with you everywhere. No one can exile you from either. Fourth, the sky.

In chapter eight he says, roughly: so long as I can look up and see the sun and moon, watch the planets rise and set, and let my mind go out among the heavens, what does it matter what ground I'm standing on?
The sky over it is the same sky that's over Rome.
Later in the letter he urges his mother to turn to study, and admits his father wouldn't let her go as far in philosophy as she wanted. It's a tender detail. Exiled, he wants her free too.

how: Some people who read the Consolation to Helvia make a habit of looking at the sky when they feel stuck or far from home, as Seneca describes doing on Corsica.

games.q: the mind's own country — tap the pairs.

s: in this letter, Seneca's mother comforts him in exile
it's the other way round: the exile writes to comfort his mother.
Seneca says the world and your own character go with you everywhere
he joins Varro's line and Brutus' line into one.
Seneca says his father encouraged his mother's study of philosophy
he admits his father held her back, and urges her to study now.

games.q: you're Seneca, exiled on a rocky island. your mother is grieving for you. what do you write?
o: describe how miserable the island is.
tell her what can't be taken from you, and that the sky is the same.
say nothing, so as not to worry her.
games.why: he wrote to comfort her: nature and character go with us everywhere, and the sky over Corsica is the sky over Rome.

practice: If you can, look out a window or step outside and look up; if not, picture the sky above wherever you are, day or night, clouds or stars.
Think of someone you love who's far away, under this same sky, and let your mind go out into it for a while, the way Seneca's did on his island.

wordCard.voice: Caelum. Latin for the sky, the heavens: from exile, Seneca told his mother that the world, his character and the sky came with him wherever he went. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: the sky, the heavens. What Seneca looked up at from Corsica.

carryVoice: Your line: the same sky. No border runs across it, from Corsica to Rome to you. See you tomorrow.
